messages.subject: Accessing logProb_Y for each mcmc samples
messages.subject_clean: Accessing logProb_Y for each mcmc samples
messages.body_plain:
Dear nimble users,

I would like to extract the log-probabilities of my observation nodes Y in my model after estimating my parameters with nimble. Ideally, I would like to have the log-probabilities for each of my observations and for every mcmc samples.
I apologies in advance if I missed that part in the manual, but I didn't find how to access them a posteriori.

Thanks for your help,

Jean-Baptiste

Here is an example of how I run nimble for my model.

M1_CPG_nimble <- nimbleModel(code= M1_CPG_nimbleCode, name= 'M1_CPG_nimble',
                               constants = constants_list, data =nimble_data,
                               inits = init_ll)
## Compile model
CM1_CPG_nimble <- compileNimble(M1_CPG_nimble)

##MCMC specification
M1_CPG_nimbleSpec <- configureMCMC(M1_CPG_nimble)
M1_CPG_nimbleSpec$addMonitors(monitored_param)

## Compile for MCMC
M1_CPG_nimbleMCMC <- buildMCMC(M1_CPG_nimble)
C_M1_CPG_nimbleMCMC <- compileNimble(M1_CPG_nimbleMCMC, project=M1_CPG_nimble)

##RUn the model
n_iter <- 10
#set.seed(0)
M1_CPG_nimbleMCMC$run(n_iter)

Samples <- as.matrix(M1_CPG_nimbleMCMC$mvSamples)

messages.body_plain:
Not a problem.  The log-probabilities for all model nodes are also stored in the model.  For node 'X', the current log-probability is stored in the variable named "logProb_X".

So if your monitored_param variable contains c('a', 'b', 'c'), then all you have to do is also add monitors for 'logProb_a', 'logProb_b', and 'logProb_c'.  Then build the MCMC, compile the MCMC, run it, and extract samples all the same, and you'll also have all the logProb variables in the resulting samples matrix.

As in your code, you could simply add:

##MCMC specification
M1_CPG_nimbleSpec <- configureMCMC(M1_CPG_nimble)

logProb_param <- paste0('logProb_', monitored_param)   #### NEW

M1_CPG_nimbleSpec$addMonitors(monitored_param)
M1_CPG_nimbleSpec$addMonitors(logProb_param)           #### NEW

.... etc

Let me know if that works for you!

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Two changes.

First -- what was causing the logProb_variables to not be recorded -- after arranging the MCMC configuration object to record the logProb variables, you were then  building the MCMC algorithm directly from the original model (which is allowable, but it uses all defaults, which does not record any logProbs), instead of building the MCMC according to your customized MCMC configuration object.

Second -- this wasn't an error, but was causing your MCMC to run very slowly -- you were running the *uncompiled* MCMC algorithm, which is a pure R function.  Instead (unless for the purposes of debugging), you should run the *compiled* MCMC algorithm, and also exact the mvSamples and mvSamples2 objects from the *compiled* version.

Both of those changes are made (and clearly indicated) in the attached file, which runs just fine.

Let us know how it goes!
Daniel

messages.subject: Trying to implement a somewhat complex multinomial model
messages.subject_clean: Trying to implement a somewhat complex multinomial model
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have two questions related to a model I'm hoping to implement in NIMBLE.  The first question regards whether I'll eventually be able to implement the full model and the second deals with sampling issues I'm having already with a partial version of the model.

1) This model involves estimating fractions of manatee carcasses that go into six categories, while accounting for uncertainty due to a seventh "undetermined" category (which might have different true fractions than the determined carcasses).  It handles this part by having two baseline fractions: one for the undetermined and one for the combined determined and undetermined (total), each with a vague Dirichlet prior.  The undetermined carcasses due to a cause are generated from a multinomial, with the undetermined fractions and the number of undetermined carcasses (for that year, region, etc.).  The total carcasses due to a cause is both the sum of the determined and undetermined carcasses from that cause, and a multinomial realization from the total fractions and carcasses.  Because this variable has both a deterministic and stochastic definition, I have not been able to implement this model in traditional BUGS languages such as JAGS.  I can implement it in PyMC, using a Potential class for the multinomial likelihood of this variable.  But I'm having convergence problems in PyMC2 and running into bugs in PyMC3.  So I was wondering if there was a way to implement it in NIMBLE, perhaps through one of the llFunction samplers.

2) The model also includes changes in the fractions during unusual mortality events (UMEs), where the mortality due to a specific cause goes up.  The baseline total mortality is an input to the model, as are the years and situations where UMEs may happen.  The baseline fractions (total and sometimes undetermined) are modified by an additional fraction factor, which is a deterministic function of the baseline total mortality and the additional mortality rate.  The additional mortality rate, in turn, is distributed as uniform.  I've tried implementing a partial version of this model, where I model the determined fractions instead of the total.  However, for any version of the model I've tried where I modify the year-specific fractions for UMEs, the baseline fractions don't get sampled, and instead stay at their initial values.  I'm using an RW_block sampler on the baseline fractions.  Any suggestions on how to get NIMBLE to sample this parameter?

I've attached sample code and data as well as a presentation that describes the model further.

Thank you for your time and any help you can provide on either question!

Jeff

messages.subject: Re: writing customized nimbleFunction
messages.body_plain:
Hi Pulong,

Thanks for your feedback.  We will try to add something to the manual to make clearer what is supported.  In the meantime, a good guideline is that if something is not explained in the manual, then it is not included.  We have a lot of plans to extend nimble to include more, and if you’re interested in contributing to development we’d be happy to help you implement some of those things.  There are a lot of competing priorities for very limited developer time and we’d be really delighted to have new contributors.

Regarding types: again what is available is in the manual.  I understand you have found it hard to get a summary of what’s available in the manual, but it’s the best resource I can point you to right now.  No, there is not support for R lists or matlab-type features.  Section 9.5.19 shows how you can create a user-defined data structure, which at the moment is nothing more than a trick of writing a nimbleFunction with setup code but no run code.

Another resource is our github wiki: https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimble/wiki.  It’s not very complete but on the right column you’ll see a preliminary list of “What works in the DSL… “ (domain-specific language, i.e. nimbleFunction run code).

Here is a modified version of your woodbury function that successfully compiles.  The main issue was that we do not yet support diag().

woodbury <- nimbleFunction(
    run = function(A=double(2), U=double(2), C=double(2), V=double(2),
        T=double(2)) {
        n <- dim(A)[1]
        AInv <- matrix(0, nrow = n, ncol = n)
        for(i in 1:n) AInv[i,i] <- 1/A[i,i]
        ##AInv <- diag(1/diag(A))
        nC <- dim(C)[1]
        Identity <- matrix(nrow = nC, ncol = nC) ## next version of nimble will have an identityMatrix function
        for(i in 1:nC) Identity[i,i] <- 1
        temp <- solve(C, Identity) + V%*%AInv%*%U
        ##temp <- solve(C, diag(rep(1,nimDim(C)[1]))) + V%*%AInv%*%U
        sol <- AInv%*%T - AInv%*%U%*%solve(temp, V%*%AInv%*%T)
        return(sol)
        returnType(double(2))
})

Please let us know further questions.  At this time of year our responses will be slower due to various travel by various nimble developers.

Best wishes
Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Pulong,

Sparse matrix stuff is on our radar screen but not yet available.

R uses BLAS and LAPACK behind the scenes, so it's already fully
vectorized and using compiled code under the hood (particularly good
if you have a fast and threaded BLAS available). NIMBLE uses Eigen for
linear algebra (apart from basic density and simulation calculates
(e.g., dmnorm) for which it uses the same BLAS+LAPACK as R).  So while
there may be some differences in speed I'd expect that NIMBLE won't
give much speedup relative to pure linear algebra calculations done
from R.

Also, you probably know this but the order of operations when you do
the matrix multiplies can matter for the Woodbury computation. You can
enforce an order using parentheses in NIMBLE run code as in R.

chris

messages.body_plain:
The following default choice of sampler is not going to work

[10]  RW_block sampler: pi[1:6, 1]
[11]  RW_block sampler: pi[1:6, 2]
[12]  RW_block sampler: pi[1:6, 3]
[13]  RW_block sampler: pi[1:6, 4]

The reason is pi has a dirichlet prior and so the elements of pi[1:nCauses,area] must sum to one. RW_block uses a multivariate Gaussian proposal and this is not going to respect the sum to one constraint. So every proposal it makes will be rejected.

You need to select or build a different sampler that respects the sum to one constraint.

Good luck
David

Hi

I am trying to explore what is and is not possible with Compiled_Model and Compiled_Mcmc_Output$mvSample  objects.

For example, once an MCMC has run, it can be desirable to take a line of the MCMC output, plug it back into the model and do something with it - perhaps simulate some dependent nodes or calculate log-likelihoods.

This is easy in R, but I can't see how to do it in a nimble function which is also to be compiled.  But, given the potential speed gain it would surely be desirable to be able to do so. I specifically mean after the MCMC has ran.

I've written a toy script based on the pump example. After running the MCMC the script revisits each MCMC sample and uses the compiled model to re-create the log-likelihood via cPump$calculate().  You can easily imagine other examples where "simulate" is used too, but I left out simulate just to keep things simple.

So the question is, is it possible to write a nimble function, & compile it, that does the same job as the loop in the script?  I can't see how to start because presumably I should be passing two pointers to the nimble function and I don't know if that is possible.

Yes, what you want to do is possible.  You can use the copy (or, equivalently, nimCopy) function to copy arbitrary nodes from a row of a modelValues object into the model. I just realized I neglected to answer your other question -- which is a good one.

>> surely everything declared in setup should be visible in the run code no?

No, not automatically.  nimbleFunctions are written to be clever enough to *inspect* the run function code (and also any other member methods, if any exist), and see what variables are used.  Then *only preserve* the setup function declarations (both setup function arguments, and variables declared in the body of the setup function) which appear somewhere in the run function (or in a member method).

So, since "model" doesn't appear anywhere in the run function, it isn't available later on.

Let's say I've written an MCMC sampler called sampler_RW_FooBar and I've put the code in two different files.

Additionally, if I reinstall nimble using my forked version, then sampler_RW_FooBar becomes available as soon as I do 'library(nimble'). So the issue is entirely about sending code from the forked directory tree to the R terminal.

Right now, my only work around is develop in the second file and transfer the code to the first at appropriate moments. But this seems redundant. I wonder if anyone else has come across this and whether there is a known work around.

David

Many thanks for your reply Chris.

The bad news is I've not been able to reproduce exactly the same behavior - although I can reproduce something not completely dissimilar and quite disturbing.

I don't know if you use emacs (just in case, C=control key, M=Alt key). With the package Emacs Speaks Statistics (ESS) I typically open an R session in an emacs "buffer" (~=a window) in one of three ways: (a) M-x R starts a new R buffer (b) C-c C-n sends a line from an R script to an R buffer, creating a new one if none exist (c) C-c C-s permits to switch the R buffer associated with a script or to create a new R buffer.

To send code from an R script to an R buffer I most typically use (1) C-c C-n, sends one line & steps (2) C-c M-r, sends a highlighted region. Another option (3) is a much longer copy and paste, i.e. highlight the code, M-w (copy), switch to the R buffer, C-y (paste).

The funny thing is, I get different results depending on if I use method (2) or method (3).

First, if working from a script in the forked code...
After method (2), typing 'sampler_RW_FooBar' in the R buffer results in the function being printed with the final line

> <environment: namespace:nimble>

Whereas after method (3), the final line prints like this...

> <environment: 0x5211ca8>

So curiously the two methods result in the code going to two different environments.

Now, working from a script that is not in a directory of the forked code...
Method (2), typing 'sampler_RW_FooBar' in the R buffer results in the function being printed with the final line
<environment: 0x4497260>
Whereas after method (3), the final line prints like this...
<environment: 0x5cfbdc8>

The environment ID numbers are unique each time you do these steps. So my layman's interpretation is that each time I do these steps the function is redefined in R and a unique environment is created for the obects within the funciton. Now for some reason, using the C-c M-r  (method (2)) approach the unique environment is not established and nimble's addSampler function returns an error

> > mcmcConf$addSampler('y', type="RW_FooBar")
> Error in mcmcConf$addSampler("y", type = "RW_FooBar") :
>   cannot find sampler type 'RW_FooBar'

If I send 'a <- 5' via method (2) from a file in the forked directory tree and the type 'a' in the R terminal it finds it.

So to conclude:
Method 2 (the fastest method I use), when used from the forked directory tree, fails to set up an environment for the function resulting in addSampler not finding sampler_RW_FooBar.
Method 3 is slower, clunkier and less ideal, but an environment is correctly assigned and addSampler can find sampler_RW_FooBar

So I'm curious what it is about this combination of git, nimble, emacs and R that results in method 2  (from the forked directory tree only) failing to do the right thing in setting up the function's environment and how that could be fixed?

David

   [?\C-r ?n ?i ?m ?b ?l ?e ?F ?u ?n ?c ?t ?i ?o ?n left home ?\C-  end home ?\C-s ?\( left ?\C-\M-n ?\M-w ?\C-c ?\C-z ?\C-x ?\] ?\C-y return])
